transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-05
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Liam Ortega (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood), Sam Chen (CTO - Nova Analytics), Aisha Khan (Lead ML Eng), Marco Ruiz (Backend Eng), Taylor Green (Platform Ops)

Summary (auto): quick SDK walkthrough, auth options, env setup, next steps to send quickstart and run bench

[00:00] Liam: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, appreciate you taking the time. I'm Liam, I'll run the quick walk—walkthrough and Priya will jump in on the SDK bits and perf.
[00:10] Sam: Yeah thanks Liam, we appreciate it. Quick note, we've been evaluating a couple options, our main asks are predictable latency under 200ms p95 for short chat completions and keeping costs reasonable.
[00:22] Priya: Got it, yeah those are, uh, pretty common. Today we'll go through the Python and TypeScript quickstarts, show auth patterns — api key service account, SSO, and then touch on env/docker examples and how you might run a simple benchmark.
[00:35] Marco: Sounds good. We run node + python microservices, so the TS and Py examples will be useful.
[00:44] Priya: Great. I'll share my screen — okay can you see the quickstart repo? it's the sample app, simple two endpoints, one client side TS call and one server-side python worker to show streaming.
[00:58] Aisha: We care a lot about streaming and K V cache behavior, we use a lot of long-context prompts. How's the kv cache handled?
[01:10] Priya: Good question — so our runtime keeps KV cache across requests when you pin a session, and the SDK exposes a session token for that. Side note: sometimes the doc generator spells it K V cache or K V cache (transcription noise) but it's the same idea.
[01:25] Liam: I'll pause, real quick: authentication — simplest path is API key in env var, e.g. REDWOOD_API_KEY or RW_API_KEY. For teams that want RBAC and short-lived creds we support service accounts with signed tokens and SSO via SAML/SAML2 or OIDC.
[01:42] Sam: For Nova we'd like SSO + service accounts for server-to-server, can you do SSO for programmatic access?
[01:48] Priya: Yes — typically customers use SSO for user access to Console, then create service accounts that are issued via the control plane and rotated. For private deployments we also integrate with customer KMS.
[02:00] Taylor: On that KMS point — we need HSM-backed keys, is Redwood compatible?
[02:05] Liam: Yep, we integrate with customers' KMS/HSM for Private. We'll share the security pack that details our integrations.
[02:12] Priya: Back to quickstart — Python example, file layout: app.py (simple POST to /generate), requirements.txt, and a small client snippet that uses redwood.Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')).
[02:26] Priya: I'll paste an example — ok, pseudo transcript of code: from redwood import Client; client = Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')); resp = client.generate(model='redwood-1-small', prompt='hello')
[02:40] Marco: Is that library published to PyPI?
[02:43] Priya: Yes, it's redwood-inference on PyPI, and npm package @redwood-inference/sdk for TS. Some customers prefer to vendor the client into their codebase.
[02:52] Sam: How do we handle staging vs prod keys?
[02:55] Jordan: We recommend separate service accounts per environment, or at minimum different API keys stored in your secrets manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager). The quickstart includes .env.example.
[03:06] Aisha: Can we set per-route quotas and token limits from the SDK or is that console only?
[03:12] Priya: You can tag requests and set policy from the control plane/Console for per-route quotas. SDK allows you to set metadata headers so Console can apply the right limits.
[03:22] Liam: Ok next the TS quickstart — typical flow: client-side TS calls your backend which holds the API key/service account, we avoid shipping keys to browser. Example uses fetch to /api/generate which proxies to Redwood via the server SDK.
[03:38] Marco: That matches our architecture. We also containerize the backend as a Dockerfile; any gotchas?
[03:43] Priya: Make sure to set the env vars at container runtime, don't bake keys into images. We included a sample Dockerfile that copies app, installs, and uses ENTRYPOINT ['python','app.py'] and relies on platform secrets.
[03:55] Sam: About latency — you mentioned dedicated capacity. If we start with hosted and it doesn't meet p95, can we move to dedicated easily?
[04:03] Liam: Yes — same API, model pinning and traffic routing is handled by the control plane. For Dedicated we provision GPU pools, and you can route traffic with the routing policy. Transition is usually a config change, but there is planning for capacity.
[04:16] Priya: Also for private/VPC we do a private control plane on customer's network, and that's a different lead time. For a two-week trial of dedicated we can usually get you ramped.
[04:26] Sam: Good. For the benchmark you mentioned, what's the best place to run it — our infra or Redwood's sandbox?
[04:33] Priya: We prefer running a benchmark from your environment (same network) to capture your real egress, but we can also run server-side tests in our sandbox. We'll provide the script and a perf checklist.
[04:44] Marco: Can the SDK stream tokens over websocket? We need sub-100ms per-token streaming for our UI.
[04:50] Priya: We support SSE and websockets for streaming; Node SDK has an example with EventSource; Python has an async streaming example. Small note: streaming latency can be affected by network and batching.
[05:02] Aisha: Speaking of batching — our workloads are mixed, some high-throughput embedding-ish calls and small chat completions. Any recommendation?
[05:10] Priya: Use our Optimize tooling — it recommends batching, quantization profiles per model. We'll show the Optimize tab in Console later — it gives batching suggestions based on observed seq len distribution.
[05:23] Liam: I'll share a link to the Optimize docs after the call, but the quickstart includes a script that toggles batching on/off so you can see perf/cost tradeoffs.
[05:35] Taylor: For audit logs and retention we need 12 months; does Redwood retain request logs?
[05:41] Liam: We retain per-contract defaults and can extend retention as an add-on. Private deployments can store logs in your S3 or logging stack. We'll include the compliance sheet.
[05:51] Jordan: Quick demo of the TS flow — I'm going to run the sample locally. (background typing) Ok calling /api/generate... response: streaming res chunk: 'Hi, Marco' — you can see the SSE event stream.
[06:10] Marco: Nice. Any rate-limit headers we should watch?
[06:13] Jordan: We return x-rw-rate-limit and x-rw-remaining in responses, and the SDK surfaces them.
[06:20] Aisha: On the auth side, do you support short-lived tokens minted by our identity provider?
[06:25] Priya: Yes OIDC-based short-lived service tokens are supported with our control plane issuing scoped credentials.
[06:31] Sam: How about L7 routing to specific model variants for canary?
[06:36] Liam: Console supports rollout policies, canary and A/B, plus automatic fallback to lower-cost model variants if latency spikes. We'll include an example policy.
[06:47] Aisha: Any pitfalls with types in the TS SDK? We consume structured responses and need TypeScript types.
[06:52] Jordan: The npm package ships types, and the SDK can generate TypeScript interfaces from response schemas. Occasionally model field names don't match exactly due to model-specific outputs; we add helpers to coerce shapes.
[07:05] Marco: Ok great. Can we get a dockerized example that shows service account auth with mounted keyfile?
[07:10] Priya: Yes the quickstart has a docker service account example: mount /secrets/service-account.json and set REDWOOD_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_FILE=/secrets/service-account.json. We'll send that.
[07:21] Sam: For our security team, besides SOC2, do you have pen test reports and a vulnerability disclosure policy?
[07:28] Liam: Yes we'll attach pen test summaries and the vuln disclosure policy in the security pack.
[07:33] (brief pause, attendees scanning materials)
[07:40] Priya: Alright let's run the end-to-end again: TS client -> backend (server SDK with service account) -> Redwood API -> stream back to client. I'm sending a small sample traffic now so you can see headers and quota.
[07:58] Jordan: The sample shows a route tag header x-rw-route: 'nova-frontend' so Console can map billing and quotas.
[08:08] Taylor: Regarding network setup for Dedicated trial, we use AWS and prefer VPC peering; are there firewall rules to open?
[08:14] Liam: For peering we share IP ranges and open TLS egress to the dedicated pool; for Private we open a few control-plane ports, details in the onboarding doc.
[08:26] Aisha: One last question — do you support model quantization configs from SDK? We do on-the-fly model switching.
[08:34] Priya: We expose model selection and quantization profile in the SDK call as parameters; Optimize can recommend profiles and you can pin them via the deployment config.
[08:44] Sam: Great, let's recap next steps.
[08:47] Liam: Recap: Redwood to send SDK quickstart repo, Docker examples, security/compliance docs, and benchmark script. Nova to share prompt set and latency SLO. We'll schedule a follow-up after you run the two-week dedicated trial.
[09:02] Sam: Sounds good. Who should I loop in for the trial provisioning?
[09:06] Liam: Loop me (Liam) and Priya, and Taylor you can coordinate infra details with our onboarding eng. We'll get a trial ticket going.
[09:15] Marco: Thanks everyone, this was super helpful.
[09:18] Liam: Thanks all, we'll send the artifacts today.

End transcript.
